headline_marked: [[HackerTube]] launched: YouTube clone built from Hacker News recommendations
headline: HackerTube launched: YouTube clone built from Hacker News recommendations
summary: A developer built a YouTube alternative using only videos recommended on Hacker News, showcasing the power of AI.
details: Frustrated with YouTube's "enshittified" algorithm and content, a developer decided to build their own video platform. The new site, HackerTube, is entirely based on videos that have been recommended by users on Hacker News.

Using an AI model named Opus 5.5 and Claude Code, the developer processed approximately 40,000 comments from Hacker News, identifying over 6,400 YouTube videos recommended across 150 topics since 2007.

The entire process, from data collection and filtering to building the YouTube-like UI and deploying it to a VPS, took approximately two hours. The developer mentioned that they no longer engage in traditional coding, relying on AI to handle most of the engineering tasks.

The only manual steps involved were obtaining a Google Cloud API key for YouTube metadata, setting up a VPS, and purchasing the domain name. The AI then handled the code deployment, security hardening, and optimization.
This project highlights a novel approach to content curation and platform development, leveraging community recommendations and AI to create a personalized viewing experience.

headline_marked: Farmer discovers [[ancient, multi-colored wheat]] in attic seeds
headline: Farmer discovers ancient, multi-colored wheat in attic seeds
summary: Italian farmer Claudio Grossi found unidentified seeds in his attic, planted them, and grew a unique wheat with seven ears per stalk and rainbow-colored kernels.
details: Claudio Grossi, a farmer from Parma, Italy, discovered a sack of unidentified seeds in his attic, believed to be left by his great-grandfather who started the farm around 1915. Despite their dry and aged appearance, he planted them in manure.

To his surprise, the seeds sprouted several types of wheat, including one that stood out with plants reaching six feet tall—twice the height of commercial wheat. This remarkable variety produced seven ears of grain per stalk, a stark contrast to the single ear typical of modern wheat.

The kernels of this ancient wheat were not only larger but also displayed a vibrant spectrum of colors, including yellow, black, red, white, and green, sometimes all on the same stem. Grossi, a lifelong grain farmer, had never encountered such a phenomenon and initially considered it a 'freak of nature'.

The discovery led Grossi to the Book of Genesis, where a passage describes a stalk with seven ears, interpreted by Joseph for Pharaoh. This biblical reference, along with other passages detailing miraculous sustenance, convinced Grossi that he had found an ancient grain, possibly from biblical times.

Grossi milled the grain into flour and baked bread, noting its unique nutty aroma and rich, sweet taste that differed significantly from commercial flour. The dough did not rise as well as modern wheat, but the final product was exceptionally flavorful.

Beyond its unique appearance and taste, the 'miracle grain,' as Grossi dubbed it, proved to be hardier and more self-sufficient. It thrived during droughts, outcompeted weeds, and required no fertilizer or herbicides, showcasing superior qualities compared to industrial varieties.

Grossi's discovery coincided with Italy's burgeoning slow-food movement, which emphasized traditional farming and natural diets. He hoped his 'miracle wheat' could help revive ancient grains and contribute to a movement reshaping how bread, a dietary staple, is produced.
